claims.text: The baseline is an equiatomic, titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy whose remaining elements each satisfy the 5–35 at% criterion.
The baseline alloy forms a predominantly single-phase solid solution.
The baseline alloy has limited intrinsic precipitation strengthening.
The intervention is incorporation of approximately 5–10 at% Mo.
Adding 5–10 at% Mo will induce finely dispersed refractory intermetallic precipitates.
The modified alloy will have a continuous high-entropy matrix containing fine, thermally stable, Mo-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mo acts as a beta-phase stabilizer in the proposed titanium- and nickel-primary alloy.
Mo promotes controlled precipitation in the proposed alloy matrix.
The proposed refractory precipitates impede dislocation glide.
The proposed precipitates improve load transfer.
Mo provides solid-solution strengthening in the proposed alloy.
The Mo-induced microstructure provides precipitation strengthening at elevated temperature.
The Mo-containing alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the Mo-free baseline.
The Mo-containing alloy will have better elevated-temperature creep resistance than the Mo-free baseline.
The expected improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance is approximately 20–30%.
The Mo-containing alloy will retain an acceptable balance of ductility.
The intervention is applicable over approximately 600–1200 °C across alloys satisfying the stated HEA composition criterion.
Mo concentrations above approximately 10 at% may cause coarse precipitates and embrittlement.
The effective Mo range depends on the other alloying elements and processing parameters.

Failure to obtain at least about a 15% improvement in both elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance, or occurrence of markedly reduced ductility or adverse microstructural evolution, would falsify the hypothesis.
